content.title: Food needs cold-chain to cut spoilage and hold shelf life
content.body: Processed foods, dairy, meat, seafood, and fresh produce all need pre-cooling, reefer transport, and controlled storage once value shifts from raw commodity to branded SKU.

content.title: Pharma requires compliance, validation, and low excursion risk
content.body: Vaccines, biologics, APIs, and specialty medicines move under documented temperature ranges, making audited handling and lane reliability part of the product requirement.

content.title: Modern retail scales SKU breadth faster than store backrooms
content.body: Organized grocery and quick-turn fulfillment centralize chilled and frozen inventory, which pushes replenishment frequency into upstream hubs and line-haul networks.

content.title: High-utilization corridors support more than rent collection
content.body: Food processing clusters, pharma lanes, and urban retail catchments fill cold rooms faster and create adjacent revenue from pre-cooling, blast freezing, grading, packing, cross-dock handling, and reefer dispatch. That service layer is what widens the gap between the two curves at **90%** [[src:est]] utilization.

slides.notes: Open with the shape of the deal, not the asset: one anchor hub secures density, then bolt-ons fill lanes and customer wallets. slides.title: The winning entry is a corridor-led buy-and-build anchored by a flagship hub, with diligence focused on utilization ramp, energy pass-through, and replacement capex

sections.heading: Start with one corridor
sections.body: The first asset should sit on a proven demand corridor where food processors, pharma distributors, QSR commissaries and modern trade already overlap, so the platform wins route density before it chases national footprint. A flagship greenfield or expansion hub becomes the operating spine: multi-temperature storage, cross-dock, reefer dispatch and value-added services in one node.

sections.heading: Use the anchor hub to lower customer acquisition risk
sections.body: A single high-spec hub lets the platform sell more than pallet space. It can bundle storage, handling, blast freezing, ripening, secondary transport and order assembly into one account, raising wallet share and making switching harder for shippers. That matters in a fragmented market because service reliability, not just price, separates scaled operators from local warehouses.

sections.heading: Build outward through bolt-ons and lane capture
sections.body: After the anchor stabilizes, add smaller leased depots, spoke facilities or tuck-in acquisitions on adjacent lanes rather than replicating full-capex hubs everywhere. This sequencing concentrates capital where refrigeration and automation matter most, while extending reach through lighter assets. The buy-and-build logic is operational, not financial engineering: common SOPs, procurement, routing and key-account coverage lift performance across the network.

sections.heading: Underwrite the ramp, not just stabilized margins
sections.body: Investment diligence should pressure-test the path from opening utilization to steady-state density by customer cohort, seasonality and lane mix. The key question is how quickly fixed refrigeration, labor and fleet overhead dilute as throughput builds. Signed base-load volumes, minimum guarantees and a credible sales pipeline matter more than brokered spot demand because early under-absorption can erase otherwise attractive mature-hub economics.

sections.heading: Treat energy and maintenance as core downside items
sections.body: Power is the most volatile operating line in refrigerated logistics, so contracts need explicit pass-through or reset mechanisms wherever customer concentration permits. Equipment uptime is equally critical: compressors, insulation, dock systems and reefer units consume replacement capital well before a facility looks old on paper. Diligence therefore needs plant condition audits, maintenance records and a grounded view of replacement capex, not management-adjusted normalized EBITDA.
